justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-sloping trajectory from roughly 85.7 at the one-day horizon to 87.0 at one month. The near-term estimate was anchored primarily by recent price momentum and the prevailing trend, assuming no major discontinuities in the immediate session. The one-week estimate nudges slightly higher on the assumption that the underlying drift continues at a measured pace, consistent with recent average directional behavior. The one-month estimate extends that drift further while also incorporating mean-reversion tendencies that tend to moderate extreme short-term moves over longer windows. In all three cases, the point estimates essentially extrapolate a gentle positive trend without assuming any dramatic catalyst in either direction.

The confidence interval widths expand predictably as the horizon lengthens, reflecting the fundamental reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the interval is relatively tight because the range of plausible outcomes is constrained by intraday volatility patterns and the short time window for news or macro surprises to accumulate. At one week, realized volatility over typical five-day windows introduces meaningfully more dispersion, and the interval widens to account for the possibility of moderate corrective moves or accelerating momentum. By one month, the interval has expanded considerably because a full range of macro developments, sentiment shifts, and liquidity conditions can materialize. The asymmetry in the monthly interval, extending further on both sides, also reflects the fat-tailed nature of return distributions over longer horizons.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data, a sudden tightening in financial conditions, or a geopolitical shock could produce a sharp selloff well below the lower bounds of any horizon. On the upside, a strongly positive catalyst such as a surprise policy easing, a blowout earnings or economic release, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices materially above the upper bounds. These tail scenarios are precisely what the 90 percent confidence intervals are designed to exclude by construction, meaning there is a residual 10 percent probability — split roughly across both tails — that the actual outcome lands outside the stated range. Liquidity conditions also matter: in thin markets, moves can overshoot dramatically in ways that volatility-based interval estimates systematically understate.
